House of pain

By: Sinethemba Nogude | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South Africa has an unknown wrestling scene — and for thirty years, these ordinary nine-to-fivers have been secretly building it, one body slam at a time.

Unique Selling Point:
Inside South Africa’s Secret Wrestling World
By day they are electricians, sales consultants, graphic designers and security technicians. By night, they become villains, heroes and champions inside a wrestling ring in Parow. Carte Blanche steps inside the bizarre, bruising and little-known world of the Africa Wrestling Alliance and the ordinary South Africans risking their bodies for a dream few take seriously.

The Hook
In a modest civic centre in Cape Town’s northern suburbs, grown men and women in face paint, leather and championship belts battle it out in front of a roaring crowd.
It looks like theatre.
It feels like sport.
It’s violent. It’s dramatic. It’s deeply personal.
And almost nobody outside this subculture knows it exists.
Is professional wrestling in South Africa just a bizarre pastime or is it a serious athletic pursuit fighting for legitimacy?
The Premise
The Africa Wrestling Alliance (AWA), founded in 1994, claims to be South Africa’s premier professional wrestling federation. With over 30 years of history, it operates out of the Parow Civic Centre , dubbed the “House of Pain.”
But what makes this story compelling isn’t just the spectacle.
It’s the people.
These wrestlers aren’t full-time entertainers earning global contracts. They are:
A quality auditor


A jewellery sales consultant


An electric fencing technician


A senior graphic designer


A travel associate


A business owner


By day, completely ordinary.
By night, they transform into characters like:
Romeo “The Chosen One” Valentino -the cocky heel


Mike “The Magnificent” Xander - the arrogant champion


Johnny “The Italian Stallion” Palazzio - the veteran people’s champ


Ed Electric -the Cape Minstrels-inspired brawler


Nicky Vex -the new-generation female heel


They train through injuries. They work full-time jobs. They perform for modest crowds. And they are chasing a dream most South Africans don’t even know is possible.


Further information:
Why This Is a Carte Blanche Story
This isn’t just about wrestling.
It’s about:
Obsession


Perceived masculinity and performance


The economics of niche sport


Body sacrifice for passion


The blurred line between sport and theatre


A subculture fighting for mainstream respect


It asks bigger questions:
Why would grown professionals risk serious injury for a side gig?


Is this sport, performance art, or delusion?


Can South African wrestling ever become commercially viable?


And what does it say about ambition in a country where opportunity is limited?


Structure
ACT 1: The Spectacle
Open on a high-energy AWA event.
Sweaty bodies slam into canvas.
Crowd chants.
Trash talk.
Blood? Maybe.
Drama everywhere.
Voiceover:
“In a hall in Parow, South Africa’s most unlikely athletes are fighting for gold… and for respect.”
Cut between the personas and their real-life identities.

ACT 2: The Double Lives
Follow key characters into their weekday worlds:


Romeo Valentino filming auditions and DJ’ing at nightclubs.


Chad Lebron selling high-end jewellery in a polished showroom.


Ed Electric installing security fencing in working-class neighbourhoods.


Nicky Vex training intensely while working in travel.
Mike Xander - the arrogant champion


Explore the physical toll:
Bruises. Sore backs. Old injuries. Spinal damage , including the founder, Shaun Koen, forced to retire after injury.
Examine finances:
Do they make money?
Who pays for costumes? Travel? Medical costs?
Is this sustainable , or sacrifice?

ACT 3: The Legitimacy Question
Professional wrestling globally is a billion-dollar machine. But in South Africa, it exists on the margins.
Why hasn’t it taken off locally?
Is there stigma?
Do people dismiss it as “fake”?
We challenge the wrestlers with tough questions:
Why should sponsors take this seriously?


Is there real athletic merit?


What are the risks?


We contrast spectacle with reality ,show the training intensity, technical skill, and choreography.

ACT 4: The Dream
The emotional core:
They want:
Television deals


National tours


International recognition


Full-time wrestling careers


But can they realistically get there?
We end on a major event - lights, music, drama - and close with the human cost behind the entertainment.


Extra Budget Items:
Car Hire
Hotel stay
flights

Cape Town

Script:


(Fan) Romeo! (Wrestler) ...Yes.

(Jayde) It’s as real as you get…

(Fans) Pick him up!

(Erin) A subculture few people know about.

(Jayd) There’s nothing fake about what we do, there is no fake way to get punched in the face.
(Wrestler) Just pick him up!

(Erin) Ordinary people putting their bodies on the line.

(Wrestler) Pick him up, pick him up.

(Erin) Sometimes paying a significant price.

(Shaun) We found that it was compression of the vertebrae in the neck, and I've now got six pins in my neck.

(Erin) This is wrestling… Cape Town style.
(Erin) In the U.S., wrestling is a billion-dollar industry with global superstars performing to sold-out arenas and massive television audiences.
(Randy Orton) I am sorry Matt, will you forgive me?
(Erin) Here, it's different.
(Subtitles) Ref, you're in the way.
(Erin) A lot smaller, a little rougher, and arguably more real.
(Erin) Driving the streets of Parow in Cape Town, it could be any suburb — quiet streets, corner shops, nothing unusual. But there’s a wrestling scene that has been building here for over 30 years. I’m about to meet the man behind it.
(Shaun) When you go back…
(Shaun) My dad was training all the professional wrestlers, and then they needed somebody to be a little bit of a crash test dummy. That's how I literally got into being on the professional wrestling side.
(Erin) I don’t know much about wrestling. But Shaun Koen does.
He’s a former wrestler, a promoter — and he’s keeping this culture alive.
(Shaun) Then of course, let’s not forget the legend himself, Jan Wilkins.
(Erin) We’re kind of trying to understand where wrestling has come from to figure out what the moment now is for wrestling in South Africa.
(Shaun) It's been very tough. Back in the 80s, it was great — everybody was going to the local wrestling, and we had eight and a half thousand people in the Good Hope Centre.
(Erin) But in the 90s, attention shifted, the crowds disappeared, and wrestling went underground.
(Shaun) More international sports was coming in, and that’s where we actually lost the footprint in the sport because we weren't getting the local coverage.
(Commentator) Wow!
(Erin) Through his African Wrestling Alliance, Shaun has built a uniquely raw and entertaining product that’s starting to draw a new audience — in person and online.
(Shaun) People that come to the wrestling, it’s people from every walk of life. Here you’ve got an attorney sitting in the front row, you’ve got a politician sitting in the rafters.
(Commentator) My goodness, wow.
(Erin) His wrestlers are mostly regular people with day jobs. They perform in four shows a year for crowds of up to 600 people.
(Commentator) Spanish Fly, Frog Splash.
(Erin) Jayd Arend is one of them — a mild-mannered graphic designer by day, a ruthless performer in the ring.
(Jayd) I kind of had to, like, decide I'm going to play somebody who embodies a lot of the things that I'm insecure about.
(Jayd) The character that I play is “The Boy” Alex Prince. He's the total opposite of me. He's cocky, arrogant.
(Erin) Do any of your colleagues know about your other life?
(Jayd) I kind of let people discover it on their own.
(Jayd) For those of you who still don’t know who we are; my name is “Pretty Boy” Alex Prince, and this is “The Outlaw” Chad Lebron.
(Jayd) So some people would see my Instagram and they'd be like, is this you? It's just this double life that I live.
(Commentator) This little three-piece that you see out here has had nothing but pure impact on the African Wrestling Alliance.
(Jayd) Sitting at a desk all day, I kind of needed an outlet just to get some of my creativity out in a different way.
(Wrestler) Alex Prince, I want you one on one at the next House of Pain.
(Nathan) The other persona is called Mike Xander…
(Commentator) Xander!
(Nathan) It's a little bit of me, but turned up to like a hundred. And I'm also very arrogant, in your face, aggressive.
(Erin) Nathan Alexander is a product auditor.
(Nathan) I used to be a very shy, quiet person. I didn't really interact with anybody. I just didn't have the best social skills. But I feel like after I started wrestling, it brought out all the confidence.
(Commentator) Superplex. The ring might collapse there.
(Erin) But there’s been a physical price to pay.
(Nathan) I tore a bicep in a wrestling match. I've broken ribs. All the slams and all that — it takes a toll. People think that the ring is like some sort of trampoline. It's not. It's wood with canvas over it, on a steel frame.
(Trainer) One, two, three…
(Erin) Shaun’s latest show is just a day away…
(Trainer) Next. Who’s next?
(Erin) …And I’ve been invited to watch a training session — at least, that’s what I thought.
(Erin) The House of Pain! I'm glad I’m not wrestling today, guys.
(Trainer) Let’s do it from the top. Get up. Now I want you to be in character. The way we do this is… there we go. He owes you rent money, he hasn’t paid you for three months, and you are very frustrated.
(Erin) After a round in the ring, I get it. Sure, the matches are choreographed, the outcomes planned — but the hits felt real.
(Erin) What do you want to say? Where’s my interview?
(Nathan) I don’t deal with…
(Erin) Dynamite comes in small packages.
(Trainer) No, no, no.
(Erin) How do we take wrestling seriously? Isn’t it all just show?
(Shaun) Yes, there is a lot of speculation. They say wrestling is a farce. Is rugby not? Is tennis not? Were they not all like McEnroe when he was playing? Didn’t he create that hype where people hated him? Because of that, we’re doing exactly the same. So where people say the guys don’t hit each other — you’re actually going to hear it.
(Erin) It’s almost showtime at Parow Civic Centre. I’m told this crowd can get rowdy.
(Jayd) Feeling this vibe, like it’s starting to get darker, the lights are going to dim. They’re going to pump some smoke in the air. Once the show gets going, there’s nothing like it.
(Announcer) Ladies and gentlemen, good evening.
(Nathan) I’ve been thrown with food. I’ve had children come and hit me. I’ve seen once an old lady walk up and kick one of the wrestlers in the [bleep] as well. So… it’s amazing. I love it.
(Erin) The action is unrelenting… and the crowd is drawn in from the first bell.
(Subtitles) Stop cheating, you’re cheating.
(Subtitles) Stop him.
(Erin) Jayd makes his entrance…
(Jayd) Look at this clown right here.
(Erin) A villain the fans love to hate.
(Subtitles) Temu muscles! Temu muscles!
(Erin) Nathan’s match is all about proving why he’s the reigning Heavyweight champion.
(Commentators) What? There we have it, we have a winner — Xander!
(Erin) How was that?
(Nathan) It was amazing. Crowd was hot, but it was amazing. I had a good time.
(Jayd) I'm completely depleted. That match took a large toll out of me, but I think we did good. What do you think?
(Erin) Yeah, I mean, you’ve got a following for sure. Jeepers.
(Erin) Having arrived here as a skeptic, I’m leaving with a newfound respect for the commitment and athleticism of the people I’ve met. The matches may be predetermined… but the sacrifice is real.
(Shaun) The biggest thing for us is, if the people are here and the wrestling is over, they don’t leave — they want to interact with all the superstars. We call them superstars because if you have a look at what they did in that ring, it makes sense.

I’ve had children come and hit me. I’ve seen once an old lady walk up and kick one of the wrestlers in the [bleep] as well. So… it’s amazing. I love it. (Erin) The action is unrelenting… and the crowd is drawn in from the first bell. (Subtitles) Stop cheating, you’re cheating. (Subtitles) Stop him. (Erin) Jayd makes his entrance… (Jayd) Look at this clown right here. (Erin) A villain the fans love to hate. (Subtitles) Temu muscles! Temu muscles! (Erin) Nathan’s match is all about proving why he’s the reigning Heavyweight champion. (Commentators) What? There we have it, we have a winner — Xander! (Erin) How was that? (Nathan) It was amazing. Crowd was hot, but it was amazing. I had a good time. (Jayd) I'm completely depleted. That match took a large toll out of me, but I think we did good. What do you think? (Erin) Yeah, I mean, you’ve got a following for sure. Jeepers. (Erin) Having arrived here as a skeptic, I’m leaving with a newfound respect for the commitment and athleticism of the people I’ve met. The matches may be predetermined… but the sacrifice is real. (Shaun) The biggest thing for us is, if the people are here and the wrestling is over, they don’t leave — they want to interact with all the superstars. We call them superstars because if you have a look at what they did in that ring, it makes sense.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): South Africa has an unknown wrestling scene — and for thirty years, these ordinary nine-to-fivers have been secretly building it, one body slam at a time.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Inside South Africa’s Secret Wrestling World By day they are electricians, sales consultants, graphic designers and security technicians. By night, they become villains, heroes and champions inside a wrestling ring in Parow. Carte Blanche steps inside the bizarre, bruising and little-known world of the Africa Wrestling Alliance and the ordinary South Africans risking their bodies for a dream few take seriously. The Hook In a modest civic centre in Cape Town’s northern suburbs, grown men and women in face paint, leather and championship belts battle it out in front of a roaring crowd. It looks like theatre. It feels like sport. It’s violent. It’s dramatic. It’s deeply personal. And almost nobody outside this subculture knows it exists. Is professional wrestling in South Africa just a bizarre pastime or is it a serious athletic pursuit fighting for legitimacy? The Premise The Africa Wrestling Alliance (AWA), founded in 1994, claims to be South Africa’s premier professional wrestling federation. With over 30 years of history, it operates out of the Parow Civic Centre , dubbed the “House of Pain.” But what makes this story compelling isn’t just the spectacle. It’s the people. These wrestlers aren’t full-time entertainers earning global contracts. They are: A quality auditor A jewellery sales consultant An electric fencing technician A senior graphic designer A travel associate A business owner By day, completely ordinary. By night, they transform into characters like: Romeo “The Chosen One” Valentino -the cocky heel Mike “The Magnificent” Xander - the arrogant champion Johnny “The Italian Stallion” Palazzio - the veteran people’s champ Ed Electric -the Cape Minstrels-inspired brawler Nicky Vex -the new-generation female heel They train through injuries. They work full-time jobs. They perform for modest crowds. And they are chasing a dream most South Africans don’t even know is possible.
metadata.Further information: Why This Is a Carte Blanche Story This isn’t just about wrestling. It’s about: Obsession Perceived masculinity and performance The economics of niche sport Body sacrifice for passion The blurred line between sport and theatre A subculture fighting for mainstream respect It asks bigger questions: Why would grown professionals risk serious injury for a side gig? Is this sport, performance art, or delusion? Can South African wrestling ever become commercially viable? And what does it say about ambition in a country where opportunity is limited? Structure ACT 1: The Spectacle Open on a high-energy AWA event. Sweaty bodies slam into canvas. Crowd chants. Trash talk. Blood? Maybe. Drama everywhere. Voiceover: “In a hall in Parow, South Africa’s most unlikely athletes are fighting for gold… and for respect.” Cut between the personas and their real-life identities. ACT 2: The Double Lives Follow key characters into their weekday worlds: Romeo Valentino filming auditions and DJ’ing at nightclubs. Chad Lebron selling high-end jewellery in a polished showroom. Ed Electric installing security fencing in working-class neighbourhoods. Nicky Vex training intensely while working in travel. Mike Xander - the arrogant champion Explore the physical toll: Bruises. Sore backs. Old injuries. Spinal damage , including the founder, Shaun Koen, forced to retire after injury. Examine finances: Do they make money? Who pays for costumes? Travel? Medical costs? Is this sustainable , or sacrifice? ACT 3: The Legitimacy Question Professional wrestling globally is a billion-dollar machine. But in South Africa, it exists on the margins. Why hasn’t it taken off locally? Is there stigma? Do people dismiss it as “fake”? We challenge the wrestlers with tough questions: Why should sponsors take this seriously? Is there real athletic merit? What are the risks? We contrast spectacle with reality ,show the training intensity, technical skill, and choreography. ACT 4: The Dream The emotional core: They want: Television deals National tours International recognition Full-time wrestling careers But can they realistically get there? We end on a major event - lights, music, drama - and close with the human cost behind the entertainment.
